Aronson’s sequence

1,4,11,16,24,29,33,35,39,45,47,51,56,58,62,64,…,1,4,11,16,24,29,33,35,39,45,47,51,56,58,62,64,\ldots,

is entry A005224 in the On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences. It comes from the self-referential sentence

T is The firsT, fourTh, elevenTh, sixTeenTh, … letter in this sentence,

which keeps track of the positions of the TT’s. Spaces and punctuation are ignored. In the English language, ordinal numbers, with the notable exception of second, contain enough TT’s to keep the sentence going on forever. Douglas Hofstadter [17] attributed this sentence to the British clinical pharmacologist Jeffrey Aronson.

The words in Aronson’s sentence generate numbers that generate words. It is a Munchausen manner to produce an integer sequence, and there are many different ways in which one can vary on this theme. Cloitre, Sloane, and Vandermast [11] considered several methods to generate self-referential sequences. We are interested in one specific type. Twenty years ago, Benoit Cloitre entered several sequences of this type in the OEIS. One of these is A086398, and its first entries are

(1) 1,5,7,9,11,15,17,21,23,27,29,33,35,37,39,43,45,49,51,53,….1,5,7,9,11,15,17,21,23,27,29,33,35,37,39,43,45,49,51,53,\ldots.

where a⁡(n)=a⁡(n−1)+4a(n)=a(n-1)+4 if n−1n-1 is already in the sequence, and otherwise a⁡(n)=a⁡(n−1)+2a(n)=a(n-1)+2, starting from a⁡(1)=1a(1)=1. Actually, the definition in the OEIS is slightly different from ours, but it is not hard to check that it is equivalent. The differences a⁡(n)−a⁡(n−1)a(n)-a(n-1) take two values that appear in some sort of rhythm, just like bouts of hiccups [4, p96], and that is why we call them hiccup sequences. We have collected many hiccup sequences from the OEIS in Table 1 below.

If we vary the definition of A086398 a bit and put a⁡(n)=a⁡(n−1)+4a(n)=a(n-1)+4 if nn is in the sequence and a⁡(n)=a⁡(n−1)+2a(n)=a(n-1)+2 otherwise, then we get A080903, which has a lot of overlap with A086398

(2) 1,3,7,9,11,13,17,19,23,25,29,31,35,37,39,41,45,47,51,53,….1,3,7,9,11,13,17,19,23,25,29,31,35,37,39,41,45,47,51,53,\ldots.

This overlap of the two sequences will be cleared up in Section 3. Another hiccup sequence in the OEIS is A064437. Robert Israel empirically found a closed formula for this sequence:

(3) a⁡(n)=⌈(1+2)​(n−1)+12+2⌉a(n)=\left\lceil\left(1+\sqrt{2}\right)(n-1)+\frac{1}{2+\sqrt{2}}\right\rceil

and checked its validity for the first hundred entries. The reader may recognize that this is a non-homogeneous Beatty sequence [14] with slope 1+21+\sqrt{2} and offset 12+2\frac{1}{2+\sqrt{2}}. Similar formulas can be found on the OEIS for other hiccup sequences.

It is possible to define hiccup sequences that are not increasing, or have first differences that take more than two values. There are plenty of such hiccup sequences in the OEIS as well. For example, the hiccup sequence A080782 produces a permutation of the natural numbers. Other examples are A079354, A080458, A080900, and A111202. A hiccup sequence with three gaps is A080574. These are all very interesting sequences, but we do not consider them in this paper. We only consider hiccup sequences that are strictly increasing. In a recent paper, Cloitre [10] has revisited his sequences and also considers non-decreasing hiccup sequences.

Our paper is organized as follows. In section 1, we define the (k,x,y,z)(k,x,y,z)-hiccup sequences and give an overview of all the results and claims that were entered into the OEIS. We prove that hiccup sequences are morphic in section 2. We use this result in section 3 to retrieve Cloitre’s recent theorem that hiccup sequences are Beatty sequences if |y−z|=1|y-z|=1 under certain further restrictions on the parameters. It turns out that (0,x,1,z)(0,x,1,z)-sequences are examples of morphic non-automatic sequences, which feature in a recent overview article by Allouche, Shallit, and Yassawi [3]. We move beyond Beatty sequences and settle a conjecture of Kimberling, combining the automatic theorem prover Walnut [19] with results of Ollinger and others on Dumont-Thomas numeration [9, 21]. In section 4 we generalize a conjecture of Bosma, Dekking, and Steiner [8] on a connection between continued fractions and Beatty sequences. We settle a specific instance of that generalized conjecture.

Abstract

In 2003, Benoit Cloitre entered a family of sequences in the OEIS that we call hiccup sequences. We collect the various claims, observations, and proofs of properties of these sequences that have been entered in the OEIS over the years, and present a unified approach, inspired by a remarkable theorem of Bosma, Dekking, and Steiner.

1 Definition, literature, and OEIS insights

We call an increasing sequence a (j,x,y,z)(j,x,y,z)-hiccup sequence if it starts at xx, and from then on, you add yy if the number n−jn-j already showed up in the sequence, and zz if it didn’t.

Definition 1 ((j,x,y,z)(j,x,y,z)-hiccup sequence).

Let a⁡(n)a(n) be a strictly increasing sequence of integers, and let j,x∈ℤ≥0j,x\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}, and x,y∈ℤ≥1x,y\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1} with y≠zy\not=z. We say that a⁡(n)a(n) is the (j,x,y,z)(j,x,y,z)-hiccup sequence if it satisfies:

a⁡(1)\displaystyle a(1) =x,\displaystyle=x,
a⁡(n)\displaystyle a(n) ={a⁡(n−1)+y,if ​n−j∈{a⁡(k)}k<n,a⁡(n−1)+z,otherwise,for ​n≥2.\displaystyle=\begin{cases}a(n-1)+y,&\text{if }n-j\in\{a(k)\}_{k<n},\\[4.0pt] a(n-1)+z,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\quad\text{for }n\geq 2.

In a recent paper, Cloitre [10] considers (0,x,y,z)(0,x,y,z)-hiccup sequences in which yy or zz can be zero. Our results partially overlap Cloitre’s, but are obtained by a different approach.

A hiccup sequence is trivial if x=z=1x=z=1. Consider, for example, the (0,1,y,1)(0,1,y,1)-hiccup sequence for an arbitrary y>1y>1. What is a⁡(2)a(2)? At index 22, the only number already in the sequence is a⁡(1)=1a(1)=1 and the next number is a⁡(3)=3a(3)=3, etc. The yy plays no role. This problem does not arise if x>1x>1, as is illustrated by the first entry in Table 1. It is the only hiccup sequence with z=1z=1 in the OEIS.

The literature on hiccup sequences is limited. Apart from Cloitre’s recent paper, the only study is by Bosma, Dekking, and Steiner [8]. It concerns the (1,1,3,2)(1,1,3,2)-sequence. Its first few entries are

1,4,6,8,11,13,16,18,21,23,25,28,30,33,35,37,40,42,45,47,…1,4,6,8,11,13,16,18,21,23,25,28,30,33,35,37,40,42,45,47,\ldots

Bosma, Dekking, and Steiner proved that there are different ways to characterize this sequence, that at first sight seem to be unrelated. The aim of our paper is to generalize their remarkable result to hiccup sequences that are strictly increasing.

Theorem 2 (Bosma–Dekking–Steiner).

The sequence A086377 can be characterized in the following equivalent ways:

  1. (1)

    Hiccup sequence – Defined recursively by

    a⁡(n)={a⁡(n−1)+2,if ​n−1∉{a⁡(k)}k<n,a⁡(n−1)+3,if ​n−1∈{a⁡(k)}k<n,a(n)=\begin{cases}a(n-1)+2,&\text{if }n-1\notin\{a(k)\}_{k<n},\\[4.0pt] a(n-1)+3,&\text{if }n-1\in\{a(k)\}_{k<n},\end{cases}

    with initial condition a⁡(1)=1a(1)=1.

  2. (2)

    Morphic characterization – The positions of 11’s in the fixed point of the morphism

    0\displaystyle 0 ↦10,\displaystyle\mapsto 10,
    1\displaystyle 1 ↦100.\displaystyle\mapsto 100.
  3. (3)

    Beatty sequence representation –

    a⁡(n)=⌊(1+2)​n−22⌋.a(n)=\left\lfloor(1+\sqrt{2})n-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right\rfloor.
  4. (4)

    Iterated function sequence –

    a⁡(n)=⌊rn+12⌋,a(n)=\left\lfloor r_{n}+\frac{1}{2}\right\rfloor,

    where r1=4πr_{1}=\dfrac{4}{\pi} and

    rn+1=fn​(rn),with ​fn​(x)=n2x+1−2​n.r_{n+1}=f_{n}(r_{n}),\quad\text{with }f_{n}(x)=\frac{n^{2}}{x+1-2n}.

We will refer to Theorem 2 as the BDS theorem. The sections in our paper are numbered according to the characterizations of this theorem. In each section we extend the BDS theorem to more general hiccup sequences.

We highlight some of the scattered comments on hiccup sequences that can be found on the OEIS. The (0,1,2,3)(0,1,2,3)-hiccup sequence is entry A007066 with first few numbers

1,4,7,9,12,15,17,20,22,25,28,30,33,36,38,41,43,…1,4,7,9,12,15,17,20,22,25,28,30,33,36,38,41,43,\ldots

It is entered in the OEIS as a Beatty sequence

a⁡(n)=⌈(n−1)⋅ϕ2+1⌉,a(n)=\left\lceil(n-1)\cdot\phi^{2}+1\right\rceil,

where ϕ=1+52\phi=\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2} is the golden mean. Except for its initial entry, it is equal to the upper Wythoff sequence A001950 plus two. It also corresponds to the positions of 11 of the fixed point of 0↦010, 1↦100\mapsto 010,\ 1\mapsto 10 that starts with 11. These facts follow from Fraenkel’s characterizations of the upper Wythoff sequence [15].

The (1,1,4,2)(1,1,4,2)-hiccup sequence A086398 starts out with

1,5,7,9,11,15,17,21,23,27,29,33,35,37,39,43,45,49,….1,5,7,9,11,15,17,21,23,27,29,33,35,37,39,43,45,49,\ldots.

Kimberling asked if it corresponds to the positions of 11 in the unique fixed point of 0↦10, 1↦10000\mapsto 10,\ 1\mapsto 1000. It is not so hard to see that this is true. The fixed point

ω=1000101010100010100010⋯\omega=1000101010100010100010\cdots

satisfies

ω=σ(ω)=σ(1)σ(0)σ(0)σ(0)σ(1)σ(0)⋯.\omega=\sigma(\omega)=\sigma(1)\sigma(0)\sigma(0)\sigma(0)\sigma(1)\sigma(0)\cdots.

The nn-th 11 in the sequence corresponds to the nn-th σ⁡(d)\sigma(d) for d=0d=0 or d=1d=1 in σ⁡(ω)\sigma(\omega). It is 44 ahead of the previous 11 exactly if the (n−1)(n-1)-th digit of ω\omega is a 11. In other words, it is 44 ahead if and only if n−1n-1 is in the sequence.

Kimberling also asked if −1<n⁡(1+3)−a⁡(n)<4-1<n\left(1+\sqrt{3}\right)-a(n)<4, which we will confirm in Section 3. There is no Beatty sequence readily available, unlike in the previous examples. Since all numbers in the sequence are odd, we can convert it by a⁡(n)↦b⁡(n)=(a⁡(n)+1)/2a(n)\mapsto b(n)=(a(n)+1)/2, which gives A026363. Here, Kimberling asks if −1<n⁡(1+3)/2−b⁡(n)<2-1<n\left(1+\sqrt{3}\right)/2-b(n)<2, which is a slightly weaker bound.

The (0,1,2,4)(0,1,2,4)-hiccup sequence is entry A080580 in the OEIS.

1,5,9,13,15,19,23,27,29,33,37,41,43,47,49,53,57,61,…1,5,9,13,15,19,23,27,29,33,37,41,43,47,49,53,57,61,\ldots

Joe Slater proves in a comment on this sequence that it coincides with the positions of 11 in the (non-unique) fixed point of 0↦0010, 1↦100\mapsto 0010,\ 1\mapsto 10 that starts with 11. By the same argument, the nn-th 11 in this sequence is 44 ahead of the previous 11 exactly if nn is not in the sequence. Otherwise, it is ahead by 22. We will call this Slater’s construction in this paper.

If we change the xx parameter from 22 to 11 we get the (0,1,1,4)(0,1,1,4)-hiccup sequence, which is the previous entry A080579

1,5,9,13,14,18,22,26,27,31,35,39,40,41,45,49,53,54,…1,5,9,13,14,18,22,26,27,31,35,39,40,41,45,49,53,54,\ldots

in the OEIS. Slater’s argument works for the fixed point of 0↦0001, 1↦10\mapsto 0001,\ 1\mapsto 1 that starts with 1010. If we change zz from 44 to 33 we get entry A080578, the (0,1,1,3)(0,1,1,3)-hiccup sequence, which by Slater’s construction is the fixed point of 0↦001, 1↦10\mapsto 001,\ 1\mapsto 1 that starts with 1010, see also [12]. Interestingly, this sequence is morphic but not automatic, as shown in example 16 of [3].

Most hiccup sequences are stand alone, but some have been linked to other seemingly unrelated sequences. In particular, A040412 has been linked to bottom-up search and A080578 has been linked to meta-Fibonacci sequences. More details on such connections can be found in Cloitre’s recent paper [10].

2 Morphisms for hiccup sequences

An increasing sequence a⁡(n)a(n) corresponds to a binary sequence b⁡(n)b(n), such that b⁡(n)=1b(n)=1 if and only if n=a⁡(k)n=a(k) for some kk. If we interpret the sequence as a set A={a⁡(n)}⊂ℕA=\{a(n)\}\subset\mathbb{N}, then the characteristic sequence is equal to 11 at position aa if a∈Aa\in A and it is 00 otherwise. We will show that the characteristic sequence of a hiccup sequence is morphic. A morphism or substitution on an alphabet is a formal rule that replaces each letter of the alphabet with a finite word over that same alphabet.

Definition 3.

Let Σ\Sigma and Δ\Delta be finite alphabets. A sequence (xn)n≥1∈Δℕ(x_{n})_{n\geq 1}\in\Delta^{\mathbb{N}} is called a morphic sequence, see [2, Ch. 7], if there exist:

  • •

    a morphism ϕ:Σ→Σ∗\phi:\Sigma\to\Sigma^{*} such that σ\sigma has a fixed point w=ϕ∞​(a)w=\phi^{\infty}(a) for some a∈Σa\in\Sigma, and

  • •

    a coding π:Σ→Δ\pi:\Sigma\to\Delta (i.e., a letter-to-letter morphism),

such that

xn=π⁡(wn)for all ​n≥1.x_{n}=\pi(w_{n})\quad\text{for all }n\geq 1.

We say that an increasing sequence a⁡(n)a(n) is morphic if its characteristic sequence is morphic.

Lemma 4.

A (0,1,y,z)(0,1,y,z)-hiccup sequence is morphic.

Proof.

We already went over this argument for z>yz>y in the previous section. Define

(4) ϕ⁡(1)=10y−1,ϕ⁡(0)=0z−y​10y−1\phi(1)=10^{y-1},\ \phi(0)=0^{z-y}10^{y-1}

and let (wi)(w_{i}) be the fixed point with wi∈{0,1}w_{i}\in\{0,1\} and w1​w2=10w_{1}w_{2}=10. That second letter 00 takes care of case y=1y=1. Since the sequence is a fixed point, we have (wi)=(ϕ⁡(wi))(w_{i})=(\phi(w_{i})). The nn-th 11 is in ϕ⁡(wn)\phi(w_{n}). It is preceded by y−1y-1 zeros if and only if the first letter of ϕ⁡(wn)\phi(w_{n}) is 11. Otherwise, it is preceded by z−1z-1 zeros. Therefore, if a⁡(n)a(n) is the position of the nn-th zero, then a⁡(n)−a⁡(n−1)=ya(n)-a(n-1)=y if nn is in the sequence and a⁡(n)−a⁡(n−1)=za(n)-a(n-1)=z if it is not. Thus, this construction yields a hiccup sequence with the desired properties. Its initial entry is a⁡(1)=1a(1)=1.

If z<yz<y, we add a letter bb to the alphabet, and define a morphism on {b,0,1}\{b,0,1\} by

(5) b↦b​0z−1, 0↦10z−1, 1↦0y−z​10z−1.b\mapsto b0^{z-1},\ 0\mapsto 10^{z-1},\ 1\mapsto 0^{y-z}10^{z-1}.

Let (wi)(w_{i}) be the unique fixed point with initial letters b​0b0. If we count bb as a 11, i.e., apply a coding b↦1b\mapsto 1, then every code word contains one 11. By the same argument as before, the nn-th 11 is preceded by y−1y-1 zeros if wn=1w_{n}=1 and by z−1z-1 zeros if wn=0w_{n}=0. ∎

The additional letter bb in the proof of the lemma, which counts as a special 11 so to speak, is needed to get the right initial condition a⁡(1)=1a(1)=1. The same trick works if a⁡(1)>1a(1)>1.

Lemma 5.

A (0,x,y,z)(0,x,y,z)-hiccup sequence with x>1x>1 is morphic.

Proof.

We add a letter bb to the alphabet and consider the fixed point that starts with bb. If y<zy<z we define the morphism

(6) b↦b​0x−2​10y−1, 0↦0z−y​10y−1, 1↦10y−1.b\mapsto b0^{x-2}10^{y-1},\ 0\mapsto 0^{z-y}10^{y-1},\ 1\mapsto 10^{y-1}.

Note that bb can be removed from this morphisms if x=z−y+1x=z-y+1, when the fixed point that starts with 00 produces the hiccup sequence. If y>zy>z we define

(7) b↦b​0x−2​10z−1, 0↦10z−1, 1↦0y−z​10z−1.b\mapsto b0^{x-2}10^{z-1},\ 0\mapsto 10^{z-1},\ 1\mapsto 0^{y-z}10^{z-1}.

Now code b↦0b\mapsto 0. ∎

Note that if we remove bb from the morphism in Equation 6, this gives the morphism in Equation 4. Similarly, if we replace b↦b​0x−2​10z−1b\mapsto b0^{x-2}10^{z-1} by b↦b​0z−1b\mapsto b0^{z-1} in Equation 7, i.e., remove the factor 0x−2​10^{x-2}1 from the image of bb, then we get Equation 5. With these morphisms for j=0j=0 in hand, we can find sequences in the OEIS that have not yet been recognized as hiccup sequences. For instance, if x=2,y=2,z=3x=2,y=2,z=3 then we get A026356. This sequence is equal to A007066, except for the first entry, which is the hiccup sequence with x=1,y=2,z=3x=1,y=2,z=3. The morphism

(8) 0↦010, 1↦100\mapsto 010,\ 1\mapsto 10

generates both of these sequences. A026356 is the fixed point starting with 00, and A007066 is the one starting with 11, see [13, Exercise 6.1.25]. That explains why the two sequences are the same, except for their initial entries.

The morphisms in these lemmas are not unique, there are other morphisms that code the same sequence. For instance, our morphism for the (0,2,4,2)(0,2,4,2)-hiccup sequence in Equation 7 is given by b↦b​10, 0↦10,b\mapsto b10,\ 0\mapsto 10, 1↦00101\mapsto 0010. This morphism can be simplified to 0↦01,0\mapsto 01, 1↦00011\mapsto 0001, which by Slater’s construction produces the same fixed point without using the special letter bb. The (0,2,4,2)(0,2,4,2)-hiccup sequence is entry A284753 in the OEIS. It is not yet listed as a hiccup sequence.

There is a degree of freedom in the morphism, by a cyclic permutation of the image words of 00 and 11. If we replace the morphism in Equation 6 by b↦b​0x−2​10y−2, 0↦0z−y+1​10y−2, 1↦010y−2,b\mapsto b0^{x-2}10^{y-2},\ 0\mapsto 0^{z-y+1}10^{y-2},\ 1\mapsto 010^{y-2}, assuming that y≥2y\geq 2, then we get the same fixed point. Similarly, we can replace the morphism in Equation 7 by b↦b​0x−2​10z−2, 0↦010z−2, 1↦0y−z+1​10z−2,b\mapsto b0^{x-2}10^{z-2},\ 0\mapsto 010^{z-2},\ 1\mapsto 0^{y-z+1}10^{z-2}, if z≥2z\geq 2. This is exactly how we got that morphism 0↦01, 1↦00010\mapsto 01,\ 1\mapsto 0001 above. If the parameters allow it, it is possible to get rid of the special letter bb by iterating the cyclic permutation. A sequence is purely morphic if there is no need for the coding π\pi in Definition 3.

Lemma 6.

A (0,x,y,z)(0,x,y,z)-hiccup sequence is purely morphic if z−y+1≤x≤zz-y+1\leq x\leq z.

Proof.

A cyclic permutation of the code words for 00 and 11 gives the morphism

(9) 0↦0x−1​10z−x, 1↦0x+y−z−1​10z−x.0\mapsto 0^{x-1}10^{z-x},\ 1\mapsto 0^{x+y-z-1}10^{z-x}.

∎

Lemma 7.

A (1,x,y,z)(1,x,y,z)-hiccup sequence with x≥1x\geq 1 is morphic. It is purely morphic if x=1x=1 and y>1y>1.

Proof.

First suppose x>1x>1. We add the letter bb and we define

b↦b​0x−2​10z−1, 0↦10z−1, 1↦10y−1.b\mapsto b0^{x-2}10^{z-1},\ 0\mapsto 10^{z-1},\ 1\mapsto 10^{y-1}.

Let (wi)(w_{i}) be the unique fixed point that starts with bb, which is coded to 00. The nn-th 11 in the sequence is in σ⁡(wn)\sigma(w_{n}). It is preceded by y−1y-1 zeros if wn−1=1w_{n-1}=1, i.e., if n−1n-1 is in the sequence, and otherwise by z−1z-1 zeros.

If x=1x=1 and y=1y=1, then we get the trivial sequence a⁡(n)=na(n)=n. If x=1x=1 and y>1y>1 then there is no need for the letter bb, and we can take 0↦10z−1, 1↦10y−10\mapsto 10^{z-1},\ 1\mapsto 10^{y-1}. ∎

Some of these morphisms correspond to entries in the OEIS that have not been recognized as hiccup sequences. For instance, the (1,1,2,1)(1,1,2,1)-hiccup sequence is the fixed point of the Fibonacci morphism 0↦1, 1↦100\mapsto 1,\ 1\mapsto 10, which gives the lower Wythoff sequence A000201. The (1,1,3,1)(1,1,3,1)-hiccup sequence is equal to A003156, and the (1,1,2,3)(1,1,2,3)-hiccup sequence is A026352. The result is not sharp. There are more choices of parameters for which hiccup sequences are purely morphic. For instance, the morphism 0↦010, 1↦010\mapsto 010,\ 1\mapsto 01, which is the reversal of the morphism in 8, generates the (1,2,2,3)(1,2,2,3)-hiccup sequence by Slater’s argument. It is the upper Wythoff sequence A001950.

Lemma 8.

Let b⁡(n)b(n) be the (0,z−1,y,z)(0,z-1,y,z)-hiccup sequence for y,z>1y,z>1, and let

a⁡(n+1)=b⁡(n)+1,a⁡(1)=0.a(n+1)=b(n)+1,\ a(1)=0.

Then a⁡(n)a(n) is the (0,0,y,z)(0,0,y,z)-hiccup sequence. In particular, a⁡(n+1)a(n+1) is morphic.

For instance, A081841 is equal to A064437 plus one.

Proof.

Since y,z>1y,z>1 we have that b⁡(n+1)≥b⁡(n)+2b(n+1)\geq b(n)+2 for all nn and b⁡(1)=z−1≥1b(1)=z-1\geq 1. It follows that b⁡(n)>nb(n)>n for n>1n>1. By definition, a⁡(2)=b⁡(1)+1=za(2)=b(1)+1=z, which is the correct value for the (0,0,y,z)(0,0,y,z)-hiccup sequence. For n>1n>1 we have

a⁡(n+1)=b⁡(n)+1=b⁡(n−1)+y+1=a⁡(n)+ya(n+1)=b(n)+1=b(n-1)+y+1=a(n)+y

if n∈{b⁡(k)}k<nn\in\{b(k)\}_{k<n}, and otherwise

a⁡(n+1)=b⁡(n)+1=b⁡(n−1)+z+1=a⁡(n)+z.a(n+1)=b(n)+1=b(n-1)+z+1=a(n)+z.

Since a⁡(k)=b⁡(k−1)+1a(k)=b(k-1)+1 and a⁡(1)=0a(1)=0, it follows that a⁡(n+1)=a⁡(n)+ya(n+1)=a(n)+y if and only if n+1∈{a⁡(k)}k<n+1n+1\in\{a(k)\}_{k<n+1}, and it is a⁡(n+1)=a⁡(n)+za(n+1)=a(n)+z otherwise.

The sequence b⁡(n)b(n) corresponds to the positions of 11 in a coded fixed point of a morphism. This morphism has an alphabet of two or three letters, depending on the parameters. To convert this to a morphism for a⁡(n+1)=b⁡(n)+1a(n+1)=b(n)+1, add a letter cc and add the substitution c↦c​dc\mapsto cd to the morphism, where dd is the initial letter of the fixed point for b⁡(n)b(n). This is the morphism for a⁡(n+1)a(n+1). Add c↦0c\mapsto 0 to the coding. ∎

Lemma 9.

Let a⁡(n)a(n) is the (j,x,y,z)(j,x,y,z)-hiccup sequence for j>0j>0 and let

b⁡(n)=a⁡(n)+j.b(n)=a(n)+j.

Then b⁡(n)b(n) is the (0,x+j,y,z)(0,x+j,y,z)-hiccup sequence.

There are two entries in Table 1 that have j=1j=1. Hiccup sequence A086377, which was considered in [8], is equal to A080652 minus one. The other entry A086398 is equal to A284753 minus one.

Proof.

By definition, b⁡(n)=a⁡(n)+j=a⁡(n−1)+y+jb(n)=a(n)+j=a(n-1)+y+j if n−j∈{a⁡(k)}k<nn-j\in\{a(k)\}_{k<n} and it is a⁡(n−1)+z+ja(n-1)+z+j if not. Now n−j∈{a⁡(k)}k<nn-j\in\{a(k)\}_{k<n} is equal to n∈{b⁡(k)}k<nn\in\{b(k)\}_{k<n}, which defines the (j,z,y,z)(j,z,y,z)-hiccup sequence. ∎

Theorem 10.

Hiccup sequences are morphic. A (0,x,y,z)(0,x,y,z)-sequence is purely morphic if z−y+1≤x≤zz-y+1\leq x\leq z or if x=1x=1.

Proof.

This is a consequence of the preceding lemmas. The sequence is purely morphic if z−y+1≤x≤zz-y+1\leq x\leq z according to Lemma 6. If x=1x=1 and y>zy>z, then z−y+1≤x≤zz-y+1\leq x\leq z. If x=1x=1 and y<zy<z, then the sequence is purely morphic according to Equation 4. ∎

This extends the second characterization in the BDS theorem. We conclude with some remarks on the morphisms that we encountered in this section. They are defined on the alphabet {b,0,1}\{b,0,1\} and the letter bb only occurs as the initial letter of the fixed point. The adjacency matrix of a morphism registers the number of letters in the substitution words. For instance, the morphism 0↦0100, 1↦1000\mapsto 0100,\ 1\mapsto 100 for the (0,1,3,4)(0,1,3,4)-hiccup sequence has adjacency matrix [3211]\begin{bmatrix}3&2\\ 1&1\end{bmatrix}. For the morphisms that we found in this section, the restriction to {0,1}\{0,1\} has adjacency matrix equal to

(10) [z−1y−111].\begin{bmatrix}z-1&y-1\\ 1&1\end{bmatrix}.

If an iterate of the adjacency matrix has all entries >0>0, then the morphism is primitive. In particular, our morphisms are primitive if y>1y>1, when restricted to the alphabet {0,1}\{0,1\}. If y=1y=1, then the morphism is not primitive.

3 Beatty sequences and beyond

By the results of the previous section, in particular Lemma 9, we may restrict our attention to (0,x,y,z)(0,x,y,z)-hiccup sequences with x,y,zx,y,z in ℤ≥1\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}. In fact, we will restrict our attention even further and consider only hiccup sequences that are purely morphic.

The semigroup of Sturmian morphisms, see [6, p. 72], is generated by the three substitutions LL, RR, and EE:

E:{0↦11↦0L:{0↦011↦0R:{0↦101↦0E:\begin{cases}0\mapsto 1\\ 1\mapsto 0\end{cases}\quad L:\begin{cases}0\mapsto 01\\ 1\mapsto 0\end{cases}\quad R:\begin{cases}0\mapsto 10\\ 1\mapsto 0\end{cases}

For instance, the square R2R^{2} produces the morphism 0↦010, 1↦100\mapsto 010,\ 1\mapsto 10 in Equation 8 which has two fixed points. One corresponds to A026356 and the other corresponds to A007066. The square L2L^{2} produces the reversal of R2R^{2} given by 0↦010, 1↦010\mapsto 010,\ 1\mapsto 01. Its fixed point is the (1,2,2,3)(1,2,2,3)-hiccup sequence, which is better known as the upper Wythoff sequence A001950.

It follows from Theorem 10, a (0,x,y,z)(0,x,y,z)-hiccup sequence is purely morphic if x≤zx\leq z and |z−y|=1|z-y|=1. We prove that the morphisms that generate these sequences are Sturmian.

Lemma 11.

A (0,x,y,z)(0,x,y,z)-hiccup sequence is Sturmian if x≤zx\leq z and |z−y|=1|z-y|=1.

Proof.

First suppose that y=z+1y=z+1. The morphism 0↦0x−1​10z−x, 1↦0x​10z−x0\mapsto 0^{x-1}10^{z-x},\ 1\mapsto 0^{x}10^{z-x} generates the (0,x,z+1,z)(0,x,z+1,z)-hiccup sequence according to Equation 9. We prove that the morphism is Sturmian. The morphisms

G:{0↦01↦01 G~:{0↦01↦10 H:{0↦11↦01G\colon\begin{cases}0\mapsto 0\\ 1\mapsto 01\end{cases}\text{ }\tilde{G}\colon\begin{cases}0\mapsto 0\\ 1\mapsto 10\end{cases}\text{ }H\colon\begin{cases}0\mapsto 1\\ 1\mapsto 01\end{cases}

are Sturmian. They are G=L∘EG=L\circ E, G~=R∘E\tilde{G}=R\circ E, and H=E∘G~H=E\circ\tilde{G}. Now Gx−1∘G~z−x∘HG^{x-1}\circ\tilde{G}^{z-x}\circ H produces the required morphism.

Now suppose y=z−1y=z-1. If x≥2x\geq 2, then 0↦0x−1​10z−x, 1↦0x−2​10z−x0\mapsto 0^{x-1}10^{z-x},\ 1\mapsto 0^{x-2}10^{z-x} generates the (0,x,z−1,z)(0,x,z-1,z)-hiccup sequence, according to Equation 9. It is equal to Gx−2∘G~z−x∘H∘EG^{x-2}\circ\tilde{G}^{z-x}\circ H\circ E. Recall that we require z>1z>1 if x=1x=1. If x=1x=1, then 0↦010z−2, 1↦10z−20\mapsto 010^{z-2},\ 1\mapsto 10^{z-2} generates the (0,1,z−1,z)(0,1,z-1,z)-hiccup sequence, starting from 11, according to Equation 4. This is the same morphism used for the (0,2,z−1,z)(0,2,z-1,z)-hiccup sequence, but starting from the other letter. ∎

There is a well-known correspondence between Sturmian substitutions and the sequences

Sα,β​(n)=⌊α⁡(n+1)+β⌋−⌊α​n+β⌋,S_{\alpha,\beta}(n)=\lfloor\alpha(n+1)+\beta\rfloor-\lfloor\alpha n+\beta\rfloor,

which are known as Sturmian words or mechanical words, see [6, p53]. The values of α\alpha and β\beta can be determined from the following transformations

TE​(x,y)=(1−x,1−y),TL​(x,y)=(1−x1−2​x,1−y1−2​x),TR​(x,y)=(1−x1−2​x,2−x−y1−2​x).T_{E}(x,y)=\left(1-x,1-y\right),\ T_{L}(x,y)=\left(\frac{1-x}{1-2x},\frac{1-y}{1-2x}\right),\ T_{R}(x,y)=\left(\frac{1-x}{1-2x},\frac{2-x-y}{1-2x}\right).

A composition of E,L,RE,L,R corresponds to a composition of these transformations, and (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) is a fixed point of the resulting composite transformation, see [6, p73] and [8]. As an example, we compute α\alpha and β\beta for the fixed point of the morphism 0↦010, 1↦100\mapsto 010,\ 1\mapsto 10. The morphism has adjacency matrix

M=[2111]M=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\ 1&1\end{bmatrix}

which has largest eigenvalue λ=3+52\lambda=\frac{3+\sqrt{5}}{2}. Now α\alpha is equal to the density of 1′​s1^{\prime}s in the fixed point of the morphism, and a minor calculation gives α=3−52\alpha=\frac{3-\sqrt{5}}{2}. The fixed point (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) for TR2=TR​TRT_{R^{2}}=T_{R}T_{R} satisfies β=1−α\beta=1-\alpha. This is one of the special cases in which rounding up or down makes a difference for the mechanical word. The rounded-up sequence corresponds to the fixed point beginning with 00, while the rounded-down one begins with 11.

Mechanical words can be converted to Beatty sequences [14]. The following result and its proof is almost identical to [8, Lemma 1].

Lemma 12.

Let α>1\alpha>1 be irrational, and let (sn)n≥1(s_{n})_{n\geq 1} be given by the rounded-up mechanical sequence

sn=⌈(n+1)​α+β⌉−⌈n​α+β⌉,s_{n}=\lceil(n+1)\alpha+\beta\rceil-\lceil n\alpha+\beta\rceil,

for some real number β\beta with α+β≥1\alpha+\beta\geq 1. Then the rounded-down Beatty sequence

⌊kα−βα⌋​ for ​k∈ℕ\left\lfloor\frac{k}{\alpha}-\frac{\beta}{\alpha}\right\rfloor\ \text{ for }k\in\mathbb{N}

corresponds to the sequence of positions of 1 in (sn)(s_{n}). Similarly, a rounded-down mechanical sequence corresponds to a rounded-up Beatty sequence.

Proof.

Since α+β≥1\alpha+\beta\geq 1 we have that kα−βα≥1\frac{k}{\alpha}-\frac{\beta}{\alpha}\geq 1 if k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}. It follows that the elements of our Beatty sequence are all natural numbers.

∃k≥1:n=⌊kα−βα⌋\displaystyle\exists k\geq 1:n=\left\lfloor\frac{k}{\alpha}-\frac{\beta}{\alpha}\right\rfloor ⟺∃k≥1:n≤kα−βα<n+1\displaystyle\Longleftrightarrow\exists k\geq 1:n\leq\frac{k}{\alpha}-\frac{\beta}{\alpha}<n+1
⟺∃k≥1:n​α+β≤k<(n+1)​α+β\displaystyle\Longleftrightarrow\exists k\geq 1:{n\alpha+\beta}\leq k<{(n+1)\alpha+\beta}
⟺∃k≥1:⌈n​α+β⌉=k​ and ​⌈(n+1)​α+β⌉=k+1\displaystyle\Longleftrightarrow\exists k\geq 1:\left\lceil{n\alpha+\beta}\right\rceil=k\text{ and }\left\lceil{(n+1)\alpha+\beta}\right\rceil=k+1
because ​α<1\displaystyle\text{\small because }\alpha<1
⟺⌈(n+1)​α+β⌉−⌈n​α+β⌉=1\displaystyle\Longleftrightarrow\left\lceil{(n+1)\alpha+\beta}\right\rceil-\left\lceil{n\alpha+\beta}\right\rceil=1
⟺sn=1.\displaystyle\Longleftrightarrow s_{n}=1.

The same argument gives that n=⌈kα−βα⌉n=\left\lceil\frac{k}{\alpha}-\frac{\beta}{\alpha}\right\rceil if and only if ⌊n​α+β⌋−⌊(n−1)​α+β⌋=1\left\lfloor{n\alpha+\beta}\right\rfloor-\left\lfloor{(n-1)\alpha+\beta}\right\rfloor=1. ∎

For instance, A007066 is given by

⌈kα−1−αα⌉\left\lceil\frac{k}{\alpha}-\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}\right\rceil

while A026356 is given by

⌊kα−1−αα+1⌋,\left\lfloor\frac{k}{\alpha}-\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}+1\right\rfloor,

for α=3−52\alpha=\frac{3-\sqrt{5}}{2}. These lemmas lead to the following generalization of the third characterization of the BDS theorem, which was recently proved by Cloitre. He provides many more concrete expressions for hiccup sequences that are Beatty sequences.

Theorem 13 (Cloitre, [10]).

A hiccup sequence is a Beatty sequence if x≤zx\leq z and y>1y>1 and |y−z|=1|y-z|=1.

Out of the 21 hiccup sequences in Table 1, there are 16 that satisfy this condition. Out of the remaining 5 sequences, 3 have parameter y=1y=1, namely (0,1,1,3),(0,1,1,4),(0,1,1,3),(0,1,1,4), and (0,3,1,3)(0,3,1,3). The morphisms that generate these sequences are not primitive, as we saw Equation 10 above. We already mentioned that the (0,1,1,3)(0,1,1,3)-hiccup sequence A080578 is a morphic sequence that is not automatic. It is example 16 in [3]. By the same argument, it is possible to show that (0,x,1,z)(0,x,1,z)-hiccup sequences are not automatic.

From the remaining two hiccup sequences that are non-Beatty we consider the (0,2,4,2)(0,2,4,2)-hiccup sequence A284753, which is a relatively recent addition to the OEIS. It is equal to 1+A086398¯1+\hrefhttps://oeis.org/A086398 by Lemma 9, and has some interesting properties. In the comments on this sequence on the OEIS, Dekking proves that it is equal to 2 times A026363. Kimberling conjectures that −2<(1+3)​n−a⁡(n)<3-2<(1+\sqrt{3})n-a(n)<3, and Dekking remarks that (1+3)​n−a⁡(n)(1+\sqrt{3})n-a(n) is bounded by a result of Adamczewski [1], where a⁡(n)a(n) is A284753. We explore the sequence with the assistance of the automatic theorem prover Walnut [19, 23].

Schaeffer, Shallit, and Zorcic [22] proved that the first-order logical theory of quadratic Beatty sequences with addition is decidable. We apply their ideas to study A284753. This hiccup sequence is purely morphic and generated by 0↦01, 1↦00010\mapsto 01,\ 1\mapsto 0001. We used Ollinger’s licofage toolkit [21], which is described in Carton et al. [9], to convert the morphism to a Dumont-Thomas numeration system for Walnut. The base of the numeration system corresponds to the lengths of the iterated substitution words

0↦01↦010001↦0100010101010001↦⋯,0\mapsto 01\mapsto 010001\mapsto 0100010101010001\mapsto\cdots,

which are equal to 1,2,6,16,44,…1,2,6,16,44,\ldots, and satisfies the linear recurrence Bn+1=2​Bn+2​Bn−1.B_{n+1}=2B_{n}+2B_{n-1}. Every number is represented by a unique word with digits {0,1,2,3}\{0,1,2,3\} that is accepted by the automaton in Fig. 1. For instance, the number 3939 is represented by 13211321 in this numeration system.

The first ten entries of the sequence are given in Table 2 in decimal and in Dumont-Thomas representation. It is now easy to guess that the Dumont-Thomas representation of the sequence is (0​w,w​0)(0w,w0) where ww runs over the admissible words with most initial digit 11. This is in line with the results of Schaeffer, Shallit, and Zorcic, who proved that such expressions describe Beatty sequences in Ostrowski numeration. It is a standard exercise to define an automaton in Walnut that recognizes such expressions, see [23, p.106]. We implemented it as shift0123 and we named the Dumont-Thomas numeration system as msd_dumthomabaaab. It is a standard task for Walnut to verify that the sequence is indeed of the form (0​w,w​0)(0w,w0) in this system.

We first test if differences a⁡(n+1)−a⁡(n)a(n+1)-a(n) are equal to either 2 or 4. The test is carried out within the Dumont-Thomas system with most significant digit (msd) first representation.

eval test1 "?msd_dumthomabaaab An,s,t (n>0 & $shift0123(n,s) &
$shift0123(n+1,t)) => t=s+2|t=s+4";

We then test if the difference is 44 if the index nn is in the sequence.

eval test2 "?msd_dumthomabaaab An,s,t (n>0 & $shift0123(n,s) &
Ek ($shift0123(k,n+1)) & $shift0123(n+1,t)) => t=s+4";

Finally, we test that the difference is 22 if the index is not in the sequence.

eval test3 "?msd_dumthomabaaab An,s,t (n>0 & $shift0123(n,s) &
(˜Ek ($shift0123(k,n+1))) & $shift0123(n+1,t)) => t=s+2";

The sequence in shift0123 passes the tests so that indeed A284753 is of the form (0​w,w​0)(0w,w0) in the Dumont-Thomas numeration system generated by 0↦01, 1↦00010\mapsto 01,\ 1\mapsto 0001.

In the introduction, we observed that the two sequences defined in Equations 1 and 2 have many common entries. The following establishes the connection between these two hiccup sequences using simple Walnut checks.

Lemma 14.

We have A284753(n)=(n)=A086398(n)+1(n)+1, and

A086398(n)={A080903​(n)+2,if the DT representation of n ends with a 0A080903​(n),otherwise.\text{\hrefhttps://oeis.org/A086398}(n)=\begin{cases}\text{\hrefhttps://oeis.org/A080903}(n)+2,&\text{if the DT representation of $n$ ends with a $0$}\\ \text{\hrefhttps://oeis.org/A080903}(n),&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}
Proof.

With Walnut, we define a new synchronised sequence a086398 that accepts one more than the term accepted in shift0123 in parallel with nn as follows:

def a086398 "?msd_dumthomabaaab Ek ($shift0123(n,k) & p+1=k)":

We can then verify that a086398 indeed accepts nn and the terms of the (1,1,4,2)(1,1,4,2)- hiccup sequence in parallel using the tests – test1,test2, and test3 where shift0123 replaced by a086398, and here we must modify our check – if one less than the index is in the sequence.

Now, for the conditional check, we define a DFA that accepts only the representations ending in a 00, followed by defining a DFA accepting nn and A080903(n)(n) in parallel.

reg endin0 msd_dumthomabaaab "(0|1|2|3)*0";

def a080903 "?msd_dumthomabaaab Es n>0 & $a086398(n,s) &
($endin0(n) => t+2=s) & (~$endin0(n) => t=s) ";

Again, we will verify that a086398 accepts all nn and the terms the (0,1,4,2)(0,1,4,2)- hiccup sequence A080903 in parallel using the same tests – test1,test2, and test3, this time replacing shift0123 with a080903. ∎

Additionally, there is a simple characterization of A080903.

Lemma 15.

The numbers in A080903 are those that end with a 11 in Dumont-Thomas numeration.

Proof.

We define a DFA accepting all the representations ending with a 11 in Walnut with the following code:

reg endin1 msd_dumthomabaaab "(0|1|2|3)*1";

This is followed by a simple check described in the statement of the lemma, which returns TRUE.

eval test "?msd_dumthomabaaab As (En (n>0 & $a080903(n,s)) <=> $endin1(s))";

∎

Now that we have a characterization of A284753 in terms of Dumont-Thomas numeration, we can address Kimberling’s conjectured bounds on the numbers in this sequence. Let λ=1+3\lambda=1+\sqrt{3} and λ¯=1−3\bar{\lambda}=1-\sqrt{3}. The following is a Binet type representation for the base BnB_{n} of our numeration system.

Lemma 16.

The basis BnB_{n} of the Dumont-Thomas numeration system for 0↦010\mapsto 01, 1↦00011\mapsto 0001 satisfies

Bn=λn−λ¯n2​3.B_{n}=\frac{\lambda^{n}-\bar{\lambda}^{n}}{2\sqrt{3}}.
Proof.

These numbers satisfy the recursion Bn+1=Bn+Bn−1B_{n+1}=B_{n}+B_{n-1} with initial condition B0=0B_{0}=0 and B1=1B_{1}=1. ∎

Lemma 17.
Bn+1−λ​Bn=λ¯n.B_{n+1}-\lambda B_{n}=\bar{\lambda}^{n}.
Proof.

This is a straightforward computation. ∎

In order to prove Kimberling’s conjecture that −3<a⁡(n)−λ​n<2-3<a(n)-\lambda n<2 we will run into the problem of bounding

∑i≥1di​λ¯i\sum_{i\geq 1}d_{i}\bar{\lambda}^{i}

over all admissible words w=d1d2⋯w=d_{1}d_{2}\cdots in least digit first format in our Dumont-Thomas numeration system. Since λ¯\bar{\lambda} is negative and less than 11 in absolute value, a straightforward lower bound is 3​∑i=1∞λ¯2​i−13\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\bar{\lambda}^{2i-1} and an upper bound is 3​∑i=1∞λ¯2​i3\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\bar{\lambda}^{2i}, since digits are at most 33. These bounds are not sharp enough. We need to work a little harder.

Lemma 18.

If w=d1​d2​d3​d4​d5​d6w=d_{1}d_{2}d_{3}d_{4}d_{5}d_{6} is any admissible word in lsd format in our Dumont-Thomas numeration system, then ∑i=16di​λ¯i\sum_{i=1}^{6}d_{i}\bar{\lambda}^{i} is minimized by 312121312121. For a word in seven digits it is maximized by 03121210312121.

Proof.

This is a finite problem that we solved numerically. The minimum rounded to three decimals is −2.424-2.424. To understand why this is the minimizing word, without going into the computation, notice that the odd powers λ¯i\bar{\lambda}^{i} are negative. We would like to maximize the did_{i} for odd ii. That is why d1=3d_{1}=3 is the logical candidate. If di>1d_{i}>1 then di+1d_{i+1} is positive, which explains why 312121312121 is the minimizer. The maximizer does the same thing, but for the even indexed digits. Its value rounded to three decimals is 1.7751.775. ∎

We write m6=−2.424m_{6}=-2.424 for the minimum, rounded to three decimals, and M7=1.775M_{7}=1.775 for the maximum.

Theorem 19.

The (0,2,4,2)(0,2,4,2)-hiccup sequence a⁡(n)a(n) satisfies

−3<a⁡(n)−λ​n<2.-3<a(n)-\lambda n<2.
Proof.

Let n=∑di​Bin=\sum d_{i}B_{i} be the Dumont-Thomas representation, for which we have a⁡(n)=∑di​Bi+1a(n)=\sum d_{i}B_{i+1}. It follows that

a⁡(n)−λ​n=∑di​λ¯ii−1.a(n)-\lambda n=\sum d_{i}\bar{\lambda}_{i}^{i-1}.

The powers λ¯i\bar{\lambda}^{i} alternate in sign and the digits are bounded by 33. It follows that

m6+3​∑i=4∞λ¯2​i−1<a⁡(n)−λ​n<M7+3​∑i=4∞λ¯2​i.m_{6}+3\sum_{i=4}^{\infty}\bar{\lambda}^{2i-1}<a(n)-\lambda n<M_{7}+3\sum_{i=4}^{\infty}\bar{\lambda}^{2i}.

These bounds rounded to three decimals are −2.667-2.667 for the minimum and 1.9531.953 for the maximum. ∎

This solves Kimberling’s conjecture that −2<n⁡(1+3)−A284753¯​(n)<3-2<n\left(1+\sqrt{3}\right)-\hrefhttps://oeis.org/A284753(n)<3. A natural question arising from this result is whether the results of Schaeffer, Shallit, and Zorcic on Beatty sequences can be extended to other hiccup sequences. More specifically, is it true that hiccup sequences are synchronized with respect to Dumont-Thomas numeration?

4 Iterated function sequences

The fourth characterization of the BDS theorem is the most intriguing. It connects Lambert’s continued fraction expansion of 4π\frac{4}{\pi} to the (1,1,3,2)(1,1,3,2)-hiccup sequence. Lambert’s expansion is given by

4π=1+123+225+327+42⋱,{\frac{4}{\pi}}=1+\cfrac{1^{2}}{3+\cfrac{2^{2}}{5+\cfrac{3^{2}}{7+\cfrac{4^{2}}{\ddots}}}},

which is a special case of his continued fraction expansion of the arctangent, see [5]. It is well known that the continued fraction converges, but that the rate of convergence is not as fast as for regular continued fractions, see [18, Table 2.3]. A shorthand notation for Lambert’s continued fraction is

4π=1+Kj=1∞⁡j22​j+1\frac{4}{\pi}=1+\mathop{\mbox{\Large K}}\limits_{j=1}^{\infty}\frac{j^{2}}{2j+1}

The fractions j22​j+1\frac{j^{2}}{2j+1} are called partial fractions and the truncated expansions 1+Kj=1n⁡j22​j+11+\mathop{\mbox{\Large K}}\limits_{j=1}^{n}\frac{j^{2}}{2j+1} are called convergents. The initial convergents are

11,43,2419,204160,….\frac{1}{1},\frac{4}{3},\frac{24}{19},\frac{204}{160},\ldots.

The numerators are A012244, but the denominators are not included in the OEIS. The convergents are defined by cutting subsequent tails from the continued fraction. These tails are given by

sn=2​n−1+Kj=n∞⁡j22​j+1,s_{n}=2n-1+\mathop{\mbox{\Large K}}\limits_{j=n}^{\infty}\frac{j^{2}}{2j+1},

starting from s1=4π=1+1s2s_{1}=\frac{4}{\pi}=1+\frac{1}{s_{2}}. Each next tail is connected to the previous tail by

sn=2​n−1+n2sn+1.s_{n}=2n-1+\frac{n^{2}}{s_{n+1}}.

The fourth characterization of the (1,1,3,2,)(1,1,3,2,)-hiccup sequence in the BDS theorem is that it is equal to ⌊sn+12⌋\left\lfloor s_{n}+\frac{1}{2}\right\rfloor. It is suprising that an iterative sequence that starts from 4π\frac{4}{\pi} produces the same result as a Beatty sequence with slope 1+21+\sqrt{2}. Bosma, Dekking, and Steiner write that they were only convinced after a numerical verification of the initial 130,000130,000 terms of the sequence.

In their proof of the fourth characterization, Bosma, Dekking, and Steiner consider the family of continued fractions of polynomial type given by

(11) k−1+Kj=1∞⁡j2(j+1)​k−1,k-1+\mathop{\mbox{\Large K}}\limits_{j=1}^{\infty}\frac{j^{2}}{(j+1)k-1},

for natural numbers kk. For k=2k=2 we have the continued fraction of 4π\frac{4}{\pi}. For k=1k=1, Beukers [7] found the following elegant expression in terms of the golden mean ϕ=1+52\phi=\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2} and η=11+ϕ2\eta=\frac{1}{1+\phi^{2}}

(12) ϕ∑n=1∞1n+η​(−1ϕ2)n=121+222+323+42⋱.\frac{\phi}{\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{1}{n+\eta}\left(\dfrac{-1}{\phi^{2}}\right)^{n}}\;=\;\cfrac{1^{2}}{1+\cfrac{2^{2}}{2+\cfrac{3^{2}}{3+\cfrac{4^{2}}{\ddots}}}}.

The numerators of the convergents of this continued fraction are A288952, and appear in a study by Genitrini et al. on tree enumeration [16]. The tails of the continued fraction in Equation 11 satisfy

(13) sn=k​n−1+n2sn+1.s_{n}=kn-1+\frac{n^{2}}{s_{n+1}}.

Expressing sn+1s_{n+1} in terms of sns_{n} this is

sn+1=n2sn−k​n+1.s_{n+1}=\frac{n^{2}}{s_{n}-kn+1}.

In the final line of their paper, Bosma, Dekking, and Steiner conjecture a remarkable relation between this iterative sequence and a Beatty sequence that has slope αk\alpha_{k} such that αk2=k​αk+1\alpha_{k}^{2}=k\alpha_{k}+1. Such a quadratic number is known as a metallic mean [24].

Conjecture 20 (Bosma, Dekking, and Steiner).

Let αk\alpha_{k} be the kk-th metallic mean and let s1s_{1} be the unique positive real number such that all sn+1=n2sn−k​n+1s_{n+1}=\frac{n^{2}}{s_{n}-kn+1} are positive, where we suppress kk in our notation of the sequence sns_{n}. The rounded-down sequence ⌊sn⌋\lfloor s_{n}\rfloor is equal to the Beatty sequence

⌊αk.n−1+αk2​αk−k⌋.\left\lfloor\alpha_{k}.n-\frac{1+\alpha_{k}}{2\alpha_{k}-k}\right\rfloor.

These are not hiccup sequences, and none of these sequences appear in the OEIS. It is shown in [8] that sn−n​α−βs_{n}-n\alpha-\beta is positive and converges to zero with order O⁡(1n)O\left(\frac{1}{n}\right), where we write α\alpha for the kk-th metallic mean, and β=−1+α2​α−k\beta=-\frac{1+\alpha}{2\alpha-k}. These constants α\alpha and β\beta can be retrieved from Equation 13 if we expand it up to order O⁡(1n)O\left(\frac{1}{n}\right) as

n​α+β+O⁡(1n)=k​n−1+nα−α+βα2+O⁡(1n).n\alpha+\beta+O\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)=kn-1+\frac{n}{\alpha}-\frac{\alpha+\beta}{\alpha^{2}}+O\left(\frac{1}{n}\right).

Equating the terms of order nn to zero gives that α\alpha is the jj-th metallic mean. By doing the same for the terms of order 11, we get that β=−α2+αα2+1\beta=-\frac{\alpha^{2}+\alpha}{\alpha^{2}+1}, which gives the expression for β\beta in the conjecture.

We extend the one-parameter family in Equation 11 to the two-parameter family

(14) u+v+Kj=1∞⁡j2(j+1)​u+v,u+v+\mathop{\mbox{\Large K}}\limits_{j=1}^{\infty}\frac{j^{2}}{(j+1)u+v},

for constants uu and vv. Its tails satisfy

sn=n​u+v+n2sn+1.s_{n}=nu+v+\frac{n^{2}}{s_{n+1}}.

If we assume that sns_{n} converges to α​n+β\alpha n+\beta with order O⁡(1n)O\left(\frac{1}{n}\right), and if we take uu to be a natural number, then α\alpha is the uu-th metallic mean and

β=v​α2−αα2+1.\beta=\frac{v\alpha^{2}-\alpha}{\alpha^{2}+1}.

The generalization of Conjecture 20 then says that the rounded down tails of the continued fraction give the Beatty sequence with slope α\alpha and offset β\beta.

The continued fraction in Equation 14 can be expressed in terms of hypergeometric functions. We are indebted to Frits Beukers for pointing that out to us [7]. The following equality follows from [20, Eq. 15.7.5].

cF12​(1,1,c+1,z)=c−z+Kj=1∞⁡j2​z​(1−z)c−z+j⁡(1−2​z),\dfrac{c}{{}_{2}F_{1}(1,1;c+1;z)}=c-z+\mathop{\mbox{\Large K}}\limits_{j=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{j^{2}\,z(1-z)}{c-z+j(1-2z)},

which converges for Re(z)<12(z)<\frac{1}{2}, It is not hard to verify that

λ⋅cF12​(1,1,c+1,z)=λ⁡(c−z)+Kj=1∞⁡(λ​j)2​z​(1−z)λ⁡(c−z+j⁡(1−2​z)).\dfrac{\lambda\cdot c}{{}_{2}F_{1}(1,1;c+1;z)}=\lambda(c-z)+\mathop{\mbox{\Large K}}\limits_{j=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{(\lambda j)^{2}\,z(1-z)}{\lambda(c-z+j(1-2z))}.

If we set

λ=4+u2,z=12−u2​λ,c=z+u+vλ,\lambda=\sqrt{4+u^{2}}\;,\;z=\dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{u}{2\lambda}\;,\;c=z+\dfrac{u+v}{\lambda},

then

λ⋅cF12​(1,1,c+1,z)=u+v+Kj=1∞⁡j2(j+1)​u+v.\dfrac{\lambda\cdot c}{{}_{2}F_{1}(1,1;c+1;z)}=u+v+\mathop{\mbox{\Large K}}\limits_{j=1}^{\infty}\frac{j^{2}}{(j+1)u+v}.

For the continued fraction in Equation 12, the parameters are λ=5,z=12−12​5,c=z\lambda=\sqrt{5}\;,\;z=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}\;,\;c=z. Beukers’ formula in Equation 12 follows from the transformation

F12​(a,b,c,z)=1(1−z)a⋅F12​(a,c−b,c,z/(z−1)).{{}_{2}F_{1}(a,b;c;z)}=\dfrac{1}{(1-z)^{a}}\cdot{{}_{2}F_{1}(a,c-b;c;z/(z-1))}.

The continued fraction is therefore equal to 5​(1−η)​ηF12​(1,η,η+1,η/(η−1))=ϕ∑n=1∞1n+η​(−1ϕ2)n.\tfrac{\sqrt{5}\;(1-\eta)\;\eta}{{}_{2}F_{1}(1,\eta;\eta+1;\eta/(\eta-1))}\;=\;\tfrac{\phi}{\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\tfrac{1}{n+\eta}\left(\tfrac{-1}{\phi^{2}}\right)^{n}}.

We now restrict our attention to one particular case of the conjecture. The lower Wythoff sequence A000201, which is the (1,1,2,1)(1,1,2,1)-hiccup sequence, is the Beatty sequence⌊n​ϕ⌋\lfloor n\phi\rfloor for the golden mean ϕ\phi, i.e., the first metallic mean. According to the generalized conjecture, if we take u=1u=1 and v=1ϕ=ϕ−1v=\frac{1}{\phi}=\phi-1, then the rounded down tails of the continued fraction are equal to the lower Wythoff sequence. We prove that the conjecture holds in this particular case. The backward recurrence for these values of uu and vv is given by sn=n+1/ϕ+n2sn+1,s_{n}=n+1/\phi+\frac{n^{2}}{s_{n+1}}, which in forward recurrence is equal to

sn+1=n2sn−n−1/ϕ.s_{n+1}=\frac{n^{2}}{s_{n}-n-1/\phi}.

It is convenient to scale the tails to rn=snnr_{n}=\frac{s_{n}}{n}, which satisfy the recurrence

(15) rn+1=nn+1⋅1rn−1−1n​ϕ.r_{n+1}=\frac{n}{n+1}\cdot\frac{1}{r_{n}-1-\frac{1}{n\phi}}.
Lemma 21.

There is a unique sequence of positive real numbers (rn)n≥1(r_{n})_{n\geq 1} that satisfies the recurrence 15. Moreover, this sequence is contained in (1+1n​ϕ,2)(1+\frac{1}{n\phi},2).

Proof.

We first prove that a positive sequence rnr_{n} must be contained in (1+1n​ϕ,2)(1+\frac{1}{n\phi},2). The lower bound rn>1+1n​ϕr_{n}>1+\frac{1}{n\phi} is required to ensure that rn+1>0r_{n+1}>0. If rn≥2r_{n}\geq 2 and n>1n>1, then

(16) rn+1≤nn+1⋅11−1n​ϕ=n2​ϕn2​ϕ+n⁡(ϕ−1)−1<1,r_{n+1}\leq\frac{n}{n+1}\cdot\frac{1}{1-\frac{1}{n\phi}}=\frac{n^{2}\phi}{n^{2}\phi+n(\phi-1)-1}<1,

which is impossible since we have already established that rn+1>1r_{n+1}>1. If r1≥2r_{1}\geq 2, then r2≤12⋅11−1ϕ=1+12​ϕr_{2}\leq\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{1-\frac{1}{\phi}}=1+\frac{1}{2\phi}, which is again impossible.

We denote the functions that produce the recurrence by

fn​(x)=nn+1⋅1x−1−1n​ϕ,f_{n}(x)=\frac{n}{n+1}\cdot\frac{1}{x-1-\frac{1}{n\phi}},

and we denote In=(1+1n​ϕ,2)I_{n}=(1+\frac{1}{n\phi},2). If n>1n>1, then by inequality 16 the image fn​(In)f_{n}(I_{n}) contains (1,∞)(1,\infty). Therefore, fn−1​(In+1)⊂Inf_{n}^{-1}(I_{n+1})\subset I_{n} and fn−1​(In+1)f_{n}^{-1}(I_{n+1}) is an open subinterval in which the end points are elements of InI_{n}. We have a descending chain

such that the end-points of each next interval are in the previous interval. Therefore the chain has non-empty intersection. We need to show that this intersection is a singleton {r2}\{r_{2}\}.

On the interval InI_{n} the derivate of fnf_{n} is bounded by below by its value in 22:

|fn′​(x)|>nn+1⋅1(1−1n​ϕ)2=1(1+1n)​(1−2n​ϕ+1n2​ϕ2)=11−2−ϕn​ϕ−2​ϕ−1n2​ϕ2+1n3​ϕ2,|f_{n}^{\prime}(x)|>\frac{n}{n+1}\cdot\frac{1}{\left(1-\frac{1}{n\phi}\right)^{2}}=\frac{1}{(1+\frac{1}{n})(1-\frac{2}{n\phi}+\frac{1}{n^{2}\phi^{2}})}=\frac{1}{1-\frac{2-\phi}{n\phi}-\frac{2\phi-1}{n^{2}\phi^{2}}+\frac{1}{n^{3}\phi^{2}}},

To prove that ⌊sn⌋=⌊n​ϕ⌋\lfloor s_{n}\rfloor=\lfloor n\phi\rfloor we need to establish that there is no integer mm in between sns_{n} and n​ϕn\phi. This is equivalent to proving that there is no rational mn\frac{m}{n} in between rnr_{n} and ϕ\phi. To do this, we need to narrow down the intervals InI_{n} that we found in the previous lemma, which is a straightforward but headache causing computation.

Lemma 22.

Let ψ=−1ϕ\psi=-\frac{1}{\phi}. For each n≥1n\geq 1 we have rn∈(ϕ+1n⁡(n+1/2)​5,ϕ+1−1/(5​n2)n2​5)r_{n}\in\left(\phi+\frac{1}{n(n+1/2)\sqrt{5}},\phi+\frac{1-1/{(5n^{2})}}{n^{2}\sqrt{5}}\right).

ϕ25​n+5​n2<1ϕ−12​ for ​n>2.\frac{\phi^{2}}{5n+5n^{2}}<\frac{1}{\phi}-\frac{1}{2}\text{ for }n>2.

The intervals JnJ_{n} are disjoint and descend on ϕ\phi, which implies that rnr_{n} is a decreasing sequence with limit point ϕ\phi. We need to show that (ϕ,rn)⊂(ϕ,ϕ+1−1/(5​n2)5​n2)(\phi,r_{n})\subset(\phi,\phi+\frac{1-1/(5n^{2})}{\sqrt{5}n^{2}}) does not contain a rational of denominator nn.

No rational satisfies 0<mn−ϕ<1−1/(5​n2)5​n20<\frac{m}{n}-\phi<\frac{1-1/(5n^{2})}{\sqrt{5}n^{2}}.

Proof.

The convergents of 1ϕ\frac{1}{\phi} are ratios of consecutive Fibonacci numbers FkFk+1\frac{F_{k}}{F_{k+1}}. By Cassini’s identity

Fk2−Fk−1⋅Fk+1=(−1)k,F_{k}^{2}-F_{k-1}\cdot F_{k+1}=(-1)^{k},

Let F2​kF_{2k} be the largest even-index Fibonacci number ≤n\leq n. We will show that m−nn\frac{m-n}{n} is closer to 1ϕ\frac{1}{\phi} than F2​k−1F2​k\frac{F_{2k-1}}{F_{2k}}, which is impossible, since its first Farey neighbor that is larger than 1ϕ\frac{1}{\phi} has denominator F2​k+2F_{2k+2}. 1−1/(5​n2)5​n2≤1−1/(5​F2​k2)5​F2​k2.\frac{1-1/(5n^{2})}{\sqrt{5}n^{2}}\leq\frac{1-1/(5F_{2k}^{2})}{\sqrt{5}F_{2k}^{2}}.

This follows from the fact that f⁡(x)=1−1/(5​x2)x2f(x)=\frac{1-1/(5x^{2})}{x^{2}} is descending for x>1x>1. ∎

These lemmas prove our result.

Theorem 24.

The sequence of rounded down tails ⌊sn⌋\lfloor s_{n}\rfloor for the continued fraction in Equation 14 with z=1z=1 and v=1/ϕv=1/\phi is equal to the lower Wythoff sequence.

This settles a particular case of the BDS conjecture. It depends on the computation in Lemma 22, which shows that the tails of the continued fraction of polynomial type with partial fractions n2n+1/ϕ\frac{n^{2}}{n+1/\phi} converge to ϕ\phi slightly faster than the convergents of its regular continued fraction. A proof of the BDS conjecture requires a conceptual explanation rather than a computation.

5 Conclusion and acknowledgements

We have extended the considerations by Bosma, Dekking, and Steiner [8] from the (1,1,3,2)(1,1,3,2)-hiccup sequence to other hiccup sequences. There is still much to be explored, most notably the conjectured relation between polynomial continued fractions and Beatty sequences.

We would like to thank Frits Beukers, Benoit Cloitre, and Slade Sanderson for useful suggestions. Gandhar Joshi was partly supported by LMS travel grant SC7-2425-18. We conclude with a table of new hiccup sequences that we encountered in our study.
